prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six opening ballots placed B012 first, but I do not treat that as the argument. The case rests on the science. The chain runs from proglucagon processing, through the identification of the truncated GLP-1(7-36) peptide as the insulinotropic form and Holst's human physiology of secretion and action, to Drucker's work on the biology of the peptide, and then to degradation-resistant agonists. That chain is mechanistically complete and has been confirmed in large randomized outcome trials. It has changed practice in diabetes and obesity and is now showing cardiovascular and renal benefit. Maturity is not in question, and the discovery is not premature. A three-person prize of Holst, Drucker and Mojsov honours the discovery of the hormone's physiology and active form. That is the scientific core, and I prefer it to a prize for a particular drug. It is also a coherent single-achievement configuration.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Priority for identifying the active peptide is contested, and Habener and others who did early proglucagon and GLP-1 work are not in the supplied credit list. Leaving out Knudsen means leaving out the people who turned a peptide with a half-life of minutes into once-weekly medicines, and that is arguably what changed patients' lives. A prize that rewards physiology while skipping the engineering will be read by some as incomplete, and a prize that includes Knudsen forces out one of the three basic scientists. I cannot resolve this from the evidence in the files. I have not independently verified the priority history, and my recollection could be wrong.

responses.point: Perlmann ranked B024 (unfolded protein response, Walter and Mori) second, behind B012 and ahead of the clinical candidates. His argument was that the pathway is conceptually clean, thoroughly confirmed over decades, and a clean two-person attribution, and that clinical translation need not be a requirement for a basic discovery.
responses.response: I agree on attribution and maturity. Walter and Mori is the cleanest configuration on the shortlist, and I put B024 fourth only because translation is less advanced, not because I doubt the science. I do not agree that its attribution advantage should push it ahead of the clinical candidates. The wider disagreement is that a clean credit list is a reason to be comfortable, not a measure of merit. The omission of Ron and the PERK arm is also a real limit that Perlmann plays down. I keep B024 as a leading alternative and as a plausible second part in a future year, but I would not put it above B012 or the targeted-therapy discovery B016.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranked CAR-T (B009) second, with Rosenberg included alongside June and Sadelain, and put BCR-ABL (B016) fourth. He stressed the originality of costimulatory receptor design and the durable remissions it produced.
responses.response: I rank B016 above B009. The target-to-drug path in chronic myeloid leukemia has more than two decades of survival data and defined the targeted-therapy paradigm, while CAR-T still has open questions on secondary malignancy, solid tumours and durability. On Rosenberg I partly disagree. His adoptive-cell-transfer work is foundational but arguably a different strand from CAR design, and including him in B009 makes the credit less clean. I accept Linnarsson's point that the missing Eshhar concept credit weakens B009 more than it weakens B016, where the weakness is the missing oncogene-biology credit. I do not think B009 is yet more compelling than B016.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranked TNF blockade (B046, Feldmann and Maini) second and called it a clear bedside-to-bench translational discovery that established anti-cytokine therapy across several immune-mediated diseases, with a clean two-person attribution.
responses.response: The impact argument is strong. TNF blockade rewrote treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and psoriasis, and Feldmann and Maini are a clean pair. I ranked it sixth, not second, because the committee has to weigh whether the contribution is a mechanistic discovery or therapeutic development, and because antibody engineering and industry roles sit beside the clinical proof of concept. Wahren-Herlenius identifies that tension herself in her own uncertainties. I would revisit its rank if she can show that the mechanistic evidence for TNF as the dominant synovial driver was independent of the drug development. Until then I regard it as a serious alternative but below B016.

responses.point: Sandberg ranked optogenetics (B022) third and argued the tool reshaped neuroscience and physiology, with channelrhodopsin discovery (Nagel, Hegemann) and neuronal deployment (Deisseroth, Boyden) as separable major steps.
responses.response: I agree that the impact on experimental biology is large, and as a neuroscientist I have seen it first hand. That is why I am cautious. A method whose credit divides across six names, with priority disputed between Boyden and Deisseroth and roles for Bamberg and Miesenboeck, is hard to fit into three people without a plainly arbitrary cut. Sandberg's discovery-versus-deployment split is the most defensible approach, but it still leaves out the earlier fly work. Clinical application is only emerging, so I place it fifth and do not support it for this year's prize.

uncertainties: How credit for GLP-1(7-36) identification should be shared, given that Habener and others are absent from the credited names and I cannot verify priority claims independently.
Whether the prize should recognise the discovery of the physiology or the development of long-acting agonists, and whether Knudsen should replace one of the three academic names.
Whether the committee would favour a two-part configuration over a single GLP-1 prize, given the three-person ceiling.
Whether B016 should be framed around the targeted-therapy concept or the specific drug, and how earlier BCR-ABL oncogene discoveries are treated.
statement.conflict_note: My profile records about twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann, a fellow committee member, on dopamine neurons, Nurr1 and autophagy. This is a collegial research connection. None of the shortlisted candidates is a collaborator of mine, and none of the work on the shortlist falls within those papers. My postdoctoral work with Paul Greengard is not connected to any shortlisted candidate. No specific conflict requiring recusal is apparent from the provided profile.
